### CORE-ACC-01: WCAG 2.2 AA

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Interfaces meet WCAG 2.2 level AA (aligned with EN 301 549), with automated checks in CI and manual screen-reader testing per release.

**Why.** European Accessibility Act for covered services; public procurement rules for schools.

**How to improve.** Add axe-core or Pa11y to CI and fix contrast, labels, focus order and keyboard access.

**Sources.** [EAA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj), [WCAG22](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [EN301549](https://www.etsi.org/standards)

### CORE-ACC-02: No flashing content

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Nothing flashes more than three times per second.

**Why.** WCAG 2.3.1. Photosensitive seizure risk.

**How to improve.** Slow or remove flashing effects; offer a 'reduce motion' setting that respects prefers-reduced-motion.

**Sources.** [WCAG22](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [EAA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj), [EN301549](https://www.etsi.org/standards), [W3C-233](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/animation-from-interactions.html)

### CORE-ACC-03: Inclusive design for children with special educational needs

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Adjustable speed and time limits, audio alternatives for text, captions, dyslexia-friendly typography options, and support for switch or keyboard-only play.

**Why.** Accessibility beyond the AA floor is what makes a learning product usable by every child.

**How to improve.** Add a settings panel for speed, audio, captions and font; test with SEN teachers.

**Sources.** [WCAG22](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-ACC-04: Moving content and sound can be paused

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Content that moves, scrolls or animates automatically for more than 5 seconds can be paused, stopped or hidden, and audio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds can be paused or muted.

**Why.** WCAG 2.2.2 and 1.4.2 (Level A), within the AA target of the European Accessibility Act. Uncontrolled motion distracts all learners and harms some.

**How to improve.** Add pause and mute controls to every auto-playing animation, video and background audio.

**Sources.** [WCAG22](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [EAA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj), [EN301549](https://www.etsi.org/standards)

### CORE-ACC-05: Colour is never the only cue

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Right and wrong answers, states and instructions are signalled by shape, text, icon or sound as well as colour.

**Why.** WCAG 1.4.1 (Level A). About 1 in 12 boys has a colour vision deficiency, so colour-only feedback fails several children in every class.

**How to improve.** Add icons or text (tick, cross, label) next to colour feedback; test screens in greyscale.

**Sources.** [WCAG22](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [EAA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj)

### CORE-AI-01: No emotion recognition on learners

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The product does not infer emotions of learners from face, voice, posture, typing or other biometric signals.

**Why.** AI Act Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition in education institutions since 2 Feb 2025.

**How to improve.** Remove emotion inference. Use explicit signals (a help button, a self-report mood picker).

**Sources.** [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [AIA-GL-PROHIB](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-prohibited-artificial-intelligence-ai-practices-defined-ai-act)

### CORE-AI-02: No manipulative AI exploiting age

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** AI features do not use subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, or exploit age-related vulnerability, to change a child's behaviour in a harmful way.

**Why.** AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)(b).

**How to improve.** Review prompts and reward logic for persuasion targets that serve engagement over learning; document the review.

**Sources.** [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [AIA-GL-PROHIB](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-prohibited-artificial-intelligence-ai-practices-defined-ai-act)

### CORE-AI-03: AI interaction and AI-generated content are disclosed

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Children (and teachers) are told, in age-appropriate form, when they interact with AI, from the first interaction and in a way that is clear and accessible. This includes chatbots, AI agents and AI avatars or characters. Generated audio, images, video and text carry a machine-readable mark. AI-made media that looks real (deepfakes) has a visible label at first view; in a story or game, the label does not have to break the experience.

**Why.** AI Act Art. 50, applicable from 2 Aug 2026. The Commission's Art. 50 guidelines (20 Jul 2026) name chatbots, agents and avatars, and read the "obvious" exception narrowly; for children, assume it is never obvious. Systems already on the market before 2 Aug 2026 must add machine-readable marks by 2 Dec 2026. The Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, assessed as adequate by the Commission and the AI Board, is a voluntary way to show compliance.

**How to improve.** Add a persistent 'AI' label on AI responses and on AI characters from the first message; add machine-readable marks (for example C2PA or watermarks) to generated images, audio and video; label realistic AI media in the interface; consider signing the Code of Practice.

**Sources.** [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [AIA-GL-ART50](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/guidelines-transparency-obligations-providers-and-deployers-ai-systems), [AIA-COP-CONTENT](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/code-practice-ai-generated-content)

### CORE-AI-04: AI inventory and no training on learners' data by default

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative, ai_assessment, ai_adaptive · Detection: manifest · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Every AI component is listed (model, provider, purpose, inputs, outputs, oversight). Provider data retention for training is disabled. Learners' data is not used to train or fine-tune models without a DPIA and a lawful basis.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 5 and 35. AI Act Art. 4 (AI literacy) and provider transparency.

**How to improve.** Create docs/ai-inventory.md and switch providers to zero-retention or no-training settings.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

### CORE-AI-05: Age-appropriate AI input and output filters

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Input and output filters are set for the target age band and the product's languages, block content unsuitable for that age, and fail safe: no answer rather than an unfiltered one. Testing before and after release is in CORE-AI-09.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(e)(f) for chatbots and companions. Best practice for any child-facing generative AI.

**How to improve.** Set filters per age band and language; send filter failures to a safe fallback message.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

### CORE-AI-06: No AI persona that simulates a relationship

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** AI characters are friendly but never claim feelings, friendship, missing the child, or exclusivity, and do not create emotional dependency (see CORE-AI-08 for conversation memory).

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 3(5)(c) and 14(1)(a)(b): such a system would be an 'AI companion' in scope, even in an educational product. DFA proposal: right to switch off relationship-simulating chatbots.

**How to improve.** Rewrite the system prompt persona; add tests that reject outputs claiming feelings or friendship.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

### CORE-AI-07: Human review of decisions about learners

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_assessment, ai_adaptive · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** No grade, level placement, certification or access decision about a learner is taken solely by automated processing. A teacher can see, explain and override it.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 22. AI Act Annex III(3) human oversight requirements from 2 Dec 2027.

**How to improve.** Make automated results provisional until a teacher confirms; show the reasons.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [AIA-OMNIBUS](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai)

### CORE-AI-08: Conversation memory is off by default

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** AI systems do not keep or reuse information from a child's previous conversations by default, except where necessary to protect the child's safety. Any memory is visible to the teacher or guardian and can be deleted.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(b) and Recital 32: persistent conversational memory with minors must be disabled by default, to prevent accumulating sensitive data and reinforcing harmful interaction patterns. GDPR data minimisation and storage limitation.

**How to improve.** Start each session without past context; if continuity is needed for learning progress, store structured progress data (e.g. skills mastered), not chat transcripts.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-AI-09: AI is red-teamed before release, re-tested regularly and monitored

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Before release, AI features are red-teamed with a prompt set per age band and language. They are re-tested at regular intervals and on every model or prompt change. After release, incidents involving children are detected, logged, assessed and acted on, with a named owner.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(e)(f) and Recitals 32 and 33. The legal duty of post-market monitoring does not apply to micro and small enterprises; CSEF applies it to every provider because the risk to a child does not depend on company size. Risk mitigations by the provider of the underlying general-purpose model (AI Act Art. 55) can be relied on in part, but are not sufficient on their own.

**How to improve.** Build a red-team prompt set per age band and language; run it in CI on prompt changes and at least each term; add an incident channel for teachers and guardians and a monthly review.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

### CORE-AI-10: An AI assistant inside a game or app is opt-in and easy to leave

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** When an AI chatbot or companion is a feature of a game, app or platform, it is not switched on automatically, not displayed prominently (e.g. not pinned at the top of contacts or the home screen), children are not encouraged to use it, and they can turn it off easily at any time.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 14(2) and Recital 34, which cover AI companions and chatbots deployed as a functionality of online games and platforms, including where in-game purchases can occur.

**How to improve.** Default the assistant to off (or teacher-enabled), place it behind a neutral help entry, and add a visible "turn off assistant" setting.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-AI-11: AI never nudges children to spend or towards ads

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** AI tutors, characters and assistants never suggest purchases, upgrades, premium content or advertised products, and are not optimised for spending or engagement time.

**Why.** KIDS Act Recital 31 names AI-enhanced nudging as a commercial tactic with particular effects on minors; Art. 14(1)(c) applies the economic transaction safeguards to AI companions and chatbots, and Recital 34 extends safeguards to chatbots inside games with in-game purchases. AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) bans AI that exploits age-related vulnerability.

**How to improve.** Remove commercial goals from system prompts and fine-tuning data; add red-team prompts that try to elicit upsell and test that the AI refuses.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj)

### CORE-AI-12: Generative features cannot depict real people

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Generative features cannot make images, video or voices of real, identifiable people, other children above all. In practice: (1) no photo, video or voice recording of a person goes into generation, and there is no face swap, voice cloning or editing of photos of people; (2) prompts that name someone on the class list, or another real person, are refused, checked against the roster inside the product; (3) uploaded images are checked for faces and refused for generation, without identifying anyone; (4) generated media is labelled as made by AI and carries provenance data; and (5) a child can report "this is about me", and that report is handled first.

**Why.** A classmate's face or voice is personal data, and nobody in the class can consent for them (GDPR Art. 5 and 6; CORE-DAT-14). The EU action plan against cyberbullying names deepfake abuse. Directive (EU) 2024/1385 requires Member States to make sexual deepfakes a crime, and the AI Omnibus adds a ban on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate content or child sexual abuse material, including nudification apps (prohibition 9, from December 2026). Labels and marks follow AI Act Art. 50 and the Commission's Art. 50 guidelines. Blocking real people at the input is far more reliable than filtering the output.

**How to improve.** Remove image-to-image, face swap and voice cloning from child-facing features; check prompts against the class roster; refuse uploads with faces for generation; add provenance metadata (for example C2PA) and a priority "this is about me" report.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [AIA-OMNIBUS](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), [AIA-GL-ART50](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/guidelines-transparency-obligations-providers-and-deployers-ai-systems), [VAW-DIR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1385/oj), [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying)

### CORE-CHT-01: Every communication channel is declared

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Every way children can communicate or act towards each other is declared in csef.yaml features and listed in the DPIA, with the service used and where data is processed. That includes text chat, direct messages, comments, voice, video and live streaming, and also channels without text: emotes and reactions, avatar names and looks, drawings and shared creations, and actions in shared worlds (building, destroying, following or trapping another child's avatar).

**Why.** Accountability (GDPR Art. 5(2)) and the DPIA require knowing every channel. Contact risks are the main reason the KIDS Act regulates online games (Recital 36). Bullying uses whatever channel exists, words or not. Undeclared channels escape every other check.

**How to improve.** Add the channel to `features` (chat, multiplayer, social or ugc) and to `third_parties`; list non-text channels too; update the DPIA.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)

### CORE-CHT-02: Report and block in every channel

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** In every channel, those without text included (CORE-CHT-01), a child can report a message, a creation or a user in one step, and block any user without the blocked user being told who blocked them. The reported content is kept as evidence for the person who handles it. What the child hears after a report is in CORE-SAF-06.

**Why.** DSA Art. 16 (notice and action) applies to hosting services. KIDS Act Art. 12(1)(d) (block without identity disclosed) and Art. 19 (child-friendly reporting). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.

**How to improve.** Add report and block actions to every message, creation and profile; route reports to a moderation queue with priority for minors.

**Sources.** [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)

### CORE-CHT-03: Moderation by people and by tools

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: high

**Requirement.** Communication is moderated by named people (a teacher in school use, trained moderators otherwise) who can hide, remove, mute and suspend, supported by automated filters for text and images in the product's languages, with rate limits against spam. The level of moderation matches the age band.

**Why.** KIDS Act Recital 36 lists cyberbullying, harassment, grooming, sexual exploitation, recruitment and radicalisation as contact risks in online games. DSA Art. 28 guidelines on moderation for minors.

**How to improve.** Give teachers or moderators hide/remove/mute/suspend powers; add a text filter (word list plus a moderation API) and image checks for uploads; add rate limits.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj)

### CORE-CHT-04: Direct messages only with approved contacts; groups only with agreement

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Nobody can start a private conversation with a child unless the child (or, under 13, the guardian or teacher) has approved that contact. Children are added to groups only with their agreement. Nobody can pressure a child into approving contact.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 12(1)(a)(c) and 12(2), applied to online games by Art. 15(1)(c) for 12(1).

**How to improve.** Restrict direct messages to approved contacts within the class or group; require acceptance for group invitations.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)

### CORE-CHT-05: No links, handles or contact details in children's messages

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Messages to and from children block or warn on external links, social media handles, phone numbers, emails and addresses, so the product cannot be used to move children to other services.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 15(2) and Recital 36 (restrict link-outs, warning messages, prevent enticing minors to other services); Art. 12(3)(c) (contact details of minors never shared).

**How to improve.** Filter URLs, handles and contact details before delivery; show a warning to the child and notify moderation.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-CHT-06: Voice, video and live streaming off by default

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Voice chat, video chat and live streaming are off by default, enabled only by a guardian or teacher for under-13s, limited to approved contacts, and children cannot host live streams by default.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 11(1) (camera, microphone) and Art. 12(3)(f) (no hosting of real-time transmissions by default). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.

**How to improve.** Default voice and video to off; add guardian or teacher activation; restrict to class groups; remove child-hosted streaming.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)

### CORE-CHT-07: Children's shared media is protected

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Images and files sent in messages are checked automatically, visible to the responsible teacher or moderator, and cannot be downloaded or forwarded by other users. Contact and account information of children is never visible to people they have not accepted.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 12(3)(a)(b)(e). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.

**How to improve.** Add image checks on upload, disable download and forwarding of children's media, and restrict profile visibility.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-CHT-08: Safeguarding procedure with a route for each kind of harm

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc, survey, ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** There is a written safeguarding procedure with a named lead. It sets a route for each kind of harm: grooming, sexual exploitation, extortion, threats, self-harm signals and radicalisation in communication; and disclosures of harm (abuse, self-harm, bullying, danger at home) in free-text or voice answers, drawings and AI conversations. It says how each is recognised and escalated, how evidence is kept, and when guardians, schools, hotlines and authorities are contacted. A disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead named by the school, never automatically to guardians (who may be the source of harm) or to peers, and the child sees in age-appropriate words where to get help now. No AI analysis scans answers for risk without a DPIA and human review. Moderators are trained and supported. Bullying between children follows CORE-CHT-15.

**Why.** KIDS Act Recital 36 names these contact risks. Children disclose in unexpected places, and a disclosure left in a log or sent to the wrong adult can put the child in danger (UN General Comment 25). National child-protection law decides who must act. Code cannot show this; it is the human side of every other communication rule. Merges CORE-SAF-11 (retired in 0.11.0).

**How to improve.** Write the procedure with the DPO and a safeguarding lead; agree a disclosure route with each school; prefer closed answers where free text is not needed; train moderators and teachers; test the procedure with a tabletop exercise each year.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [BIK](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-better-internet-kids)

### CORE-CHT-09: Messages are kept only as long as needed

**SHOULD** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Messages have a defined retention period enforced by code, children and teachers can delete them, and reported messages are preserved only for the investigation.

**Why.** GDPR storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) and erasure (Art. 17).

**How to improve.** Add a retention job for messages and keep reported messages in a separate, access-controlled store.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-CHT-10: Reports stay confidential

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Do not show who reported. The reported child, other children and their guardians are never told who made a report, and nothing in the product lets them work it out: no "reported by" label, no shared report count, no action timed to point at one child. Only the person handling the report, and the safeguarding lead where needed, can see the reporter. If the school's procedure later needs the reporter's name, the reporter and their guardian are told first.

**Why.** Fear of being found out stops children from reporting. The EDPB says notice mechanisms should allow, but not require, identifying the notifier, and reveal the identity to the affected user only where strictly necessary. The KIDS Act proposal already protects the identity of whoever blocks (Art. 12(1)(d)), but no law says the same for every product's reports, so this is a SHOULD.

**How to improve.** Remove reporter names from every view the reported child or peers can see; batch or delay visible moderation actions; limit reporter identity to the moderator role.

**Sources.** [EDPB-DSAGDPR](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-09/edpb_guidelines_202503_interplay-dsa-gdpr_v1_en.pdf), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-CHT-11: Children can report for a friend; misuse is handled by people

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** A child can report something that happens to someone else ("this is happening to a friend"), from the same place as any report, without the friend's permission and without proof. The friend is offered help privately, and the report follows CORE-SAF-06 and CORE-CHT-10. Good practice: (1) the flow asks what happened, nothing more; (2) a report made in good faith that turns out unfounded never counts against the child; (3) only repeated reports that a person finds manifestly unfounded are recorded, seen only by the moderator or teacher and never by other children; (4) the child first gets a kind warning that explains why, before any limit; (5) there are no automatic sanctions; and (6) many reports against the same child by a group are treated as a possible sign of bullying, not as proof against that child.

**Why.** Bystanders often see what adults do not, and the EU action plan against cyberbullying asks that reporting and support reach bystanders. DSA Art. 23 lets online platforms, after a warning, stop handling notices from people who often send manifestly unfounded ones; for children the answer is a conversation with an adult, not a penalty. Reporting itself can be used to bully, so patterns matter more than counts.

**How to improve.** Add "this is happening to someone else" to the report flow and a private help message for the friend; record manifestly unfounded reports for the moderator only, with a warning step and no automatic sanctions; flag group reports against one child for review.

**Sources.** [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying), [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-CHT-12: No design that lets children exclude, rank or expose each other

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The design gives children no tools to exclude, rank or expose each other: (1) no voting a child out of a game, team or group, and no removal of players by other players; only the teacher or a moderator can remove; (2) no ratings of children by children (stars, scores or likes on a person, "best" or "worst" player votes); feedback on someone's work uses preset kind options or a rubric the teacher can see; (3) no polls or questions about classmates; (4) teams and pairs are made by the teacher or by the product (at random or balanced), never picked by children in front of others, and nobody sees the order of choice; (5) paid or premium items do not show status to classmates, and the school can turn their display off; (6) friend lists, friend counts and online status are not shown to other children; and (7) the teacher can keep two children apart in pairings and groups without anyone seeing why.

**Why.** The EU common definition of cyberbullying includes social exclusion. Most cyberbullying comes from peers the child knows from school, so closed class groups keep strangers out but not the bully. Design that lets children vote others out, rate each other or show status hands them that power. Not law as such, so a SHOULD. Related: CORE-SAF-10 (no follower counts or likes on appearance), C-ENG-02 (leaderboards).

**How to improve.** Replace vote-kick with removal by the teacher or a moderator; remove ratings of people and polls about classmates; make teams by teacher choice or at random; hide paid status and friend counts in school use; add a "keep apart" setting for teachers.

**Sources.** [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [R-JUVONEN2008](https://www.cdmc.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/170/2018/05/sheva-3.pdf), [R-WOLKE2017](https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00787-017-0954-6)

### CORE-CHT-13: Children can keep evidence and reach national help

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** A child who reports can keep a record of what happened inside the product (what was said or done, when, by which account), see it later and share it with a trusted adult, the school or a helpline, without downloading or forwarding other children's media (CORE-CHT-07). The product links to the national child helpline (116 111) and Safer Internet Centre, and connects its reporting and support to the EU online safety app through the app's interface where the country offers it. The record follows the retention rules (CORE-CHT-09).

**Why.** The EU action plan against cyberbullying plans an app where children report to a national helpline, store and pass on evidence and get help, and which platforms can connect to their reporting and support tools through APIs. The KIDS Act proposal asks Member States for free, confidential national channels that complement providers' reporting tools. Not yet an obligation for providers, so a SHOULD.

**How to improve.** Add a "my reports" view with the evidence record and a share option to a trusted adult or helpline; add national helpline links; plan the connection to the national app.

**Sources.** [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [BIK](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-better-internet-kids)

### CORE-CHT-14: Communication is open only when someone can respond

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The product says who handles reports (the teacher, the provider's moderators or both), in which hours and languages, and how fast: for example urgent safety reports within one hour and other reports within one school day while communication is open. Outside those hours communication is closed, limited to preset messages, or covered by the provider's moderators. Teachers can set open hours for their class. A child who reports is told when to expect an answer. The cover is declared in csef.yaml (`moderation`) and checked against real response times.

**Why.** A report nobody reads protects nobody. When the teacher is the moderator, chat that stays open in the evening has no one behind it. KIDS Act Art. 19 and the DSA Art. 28 guidelines expect reports to be handled promptly. CORE-CHT-03 names the people; this rule makes sure their time covers the hours the channel is open. What the product can safely offer depends on who can respond.

**How to improve.** Add open hours set by the teacher; close or limit communication outside covered hours; declare `moderation` in csef.yaml and measure response times.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying)

### CORE-CHT-15: Bullying between children follows the school's procedure, or a default one

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Strongly recommended. A report about bullying between children goes to the person named in the school's anti-bullying plan or procedure, not to the authorities and not straight to guardians. If the school has no plan, the product offers a default procedure that the school accepts at set-up (templates/bullying-procedure.md): who is told, how to listen to both children, how to keep them apart in the product (CORE-CHT-12), how guardians are informed through the school, when to check again, and when it becomes a safeguarding matter (CORE-CHT-08). Report categories follow the EU common definition of cyberbullying (humiliating, excluding, abusing, harassing or harming, once or repeated) in words for children, and the school sees totals per category for its classes, never figures that point to one child (at least 5 per figure, as in CORE-DAT-17).

**Why.** Most online bullying is between children who know each other from school, so the school is usually the right place to act. Many schools have an anti-bullying plan (in Portugal, "Escola Sem Bullying. Escola Sem Violência"), but not all, so the product must work without one. Shared categories let schools and Member States compare data, as the EU action plan asks. Not law, so a SHOULD, but strongly recommended for any product with communication.

**How to improve.** Ask at set-up for the school's anti-bullying contact, or for acceptance of the default procedure; route bullying reports there; use the EU-definition categories; give schools totals by class and school.

**Sources.** [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [R-JUVONEN2008](https://www.cdmc.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/170/2018/05/sheva-3.pdf)

### CORE-CNT-01: Asset provenance and licences recorded

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Every image, sound, font and AI-generated asset has a recorded source, licence, author and, for AI assets, the model used.

**Why.** Copyright compliance and AI Act Art. 50 marking of generated content.

**How to improve.** Keep an assets/PROVENANCE.csv and check it in CI.

**Sources.** [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

### CORE-CNT-02: Age rating self-assessment

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** The product has a documented age-appropriateness assessment covering violence, fear, language, in-app purchases, contact risks and addictive features (PEGI-style descriptors).

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 16 and 17 foresee harmonised age ratings covering monetisation and contact risks.

**How to improve.** Run a PEGI-style self-assessment and publish the resulting age and descriptors.

**Sources.** [PEGI](https://pegi.info), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-COM-01: No advertising or ad tracking SDKs

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** No advertising based on profiling of minors and no ad, attribution or fingerprinting SDKs in products used by minors.

**Why.** DSA Art. 28(2) bans profiling-based ads to minors on online platforms. The DFA proposal extends this to all traders.

**How to improve.** Remove the SDK. If marketing attribution is needed, measure it on the adult-facing website only.

**Sources.** [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-COM-02: Third-party analytics and session recording reviewed

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Product analytics and session-replay tools are either self-hosted in the EEA or bound by a processor agreement that forbids reuse of data. Session recording is not used on child-facing screens.

**Why.** Many analytics vendors reuse data for their own purposes, which would make them controllers (GDPR Art. 28).

**How to improve.** Prefer self-hosted analytics (e.g. EU-hosted PostHog or Matomo) with IP anonymisation; remove session replay from child screens.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)

### CORE-COM-03: No dark patterns

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** No fake urgency or scarcity, confirmshaming, pre-ticked options, nagging after a choice, obstruction to leave or cancel, fake notifications, or confusing double negatives.

**Why.** DSA Art. 25, UCPD. The CPC Network's 2026 Joint Statement names misleading countdown timers and false scarcity in games. The DFA proposal blacklists these in all circumstances.

**How to improve.** Rewrite the copy neutrally, remove timers and pre-selected options, make 'no' as easy as 'yes'.

**Sources.** [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj), [CPC-JS](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act), [R-RADESKY2022](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/design-tricks-commonly-used-monetize-young-childrens-app-use)

### CORE-COM-04: Purchases are adult-facing only

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Children are never directly exhorted to buy, or to ask adults to buy for them, and any purchase flow is behind an adult gate (guardian or school account), with the price in real currency. This applies to any product likely to appeal to children, even if it is not aimed at them, and an age gate does not remove the duty. Spending real money is off by default, and parental controls work, with defaults that suit the age.

**Why.** UCPD Annex I point 28 (direct exhortation to children). KIDS Act Art. 13 and 14(1)(c). CPC Key Principle 7: children are always vulnerable, and age gates do not reduce the trader's responsibility. The CPC Network's 2026 Joint Statement found games that still urge children to buy.

**How to improve.** Move purchases to a guardian or school portal; remove buy prompts from child screens.

**Sources.** [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj), [CPC-VC](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [CPC-JS](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act)

### CORE-COM-05: Purchases are labelled as purchases, in real time

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: purchases · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Before any purchase or spending of purchasable currency, the child is told in clear, age-appropriate words (and icons or audio for non-readers) that this is a purchase that costs real money, at the moment it happens, with the price in the national currency.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 13(1) and Recital 31: minors often do not understand the consequences of online transactions, so purchases must be labelled as economic transactions in real time. Binding for social and video services and AI chatbots (Art. 14(1)(c)); applied to games and learning apps as good practice.

**How to improve.** Add a purchase confirmation screen for child accounts that says "This costs money" with the euro price and requires an adult step.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj), [CPC-VC](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act)

### CORE-COM-06: No design for impulsive or unwanted spending

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: purchases · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** No one-tap or in-content purchases for children. There is a clear separation and friction between learning or play content and buying anything related to it (for example a separate adult area and a confirmation step). No spending prompts at moments of frustration, failure or excitement.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 13(2) and Recital 31: services must not be designed in a way that leads to excessive, impulsive or unwanted spending, including through separation or friction between content and purchases. CPC Key Principle 7 asks for purchase prompts clearly separate from gameplay, and holds business models that depend on a few heavy spenders to a stricter fairness standard. DFA proposal targets the same practices.

**How to improve.** Move every purchase out of the child experience into a guardian or school area; remove purchase buttons from gameplay, results and failure screens.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act), [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj), [CPC-VC](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [R-RADESKY2022](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/design-tricks-commonly-used-monetize-young-childrens-app-use)

### CORE-COM-07: No disguised advertising

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Paid promotion is never presented as learning content, game content or a character's own opinion. Any sponsorship, product placement or brand partnership is clearly identified as such, in words a child of the target age understands.

**Why.** UCPD Annex I point 11 bans editorial content paid for by a trader without making that clear, and point 28 bans direct exhortations to children to buy. DSA Art. 26 requires ads on platforms to be clearly identifiable. KIDS Act Recital 31 names product placement, influencer marketing and sponsorship as tactics with particular persuasive effects on minors.

**How to improve.** Label any commercial content clearly (e.g. "Ad" or "Paid partnership" with an icon); remove promotion voiced by characters or tutors.

**Sources.** [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj), [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-COM-08: No commercial content inside learning activities for children

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Learning activities for children contain no product placement, branded rewards, sponsored characters or influencer endorsements, even when labelled. Funding and partner credits, if any, appear only in adult-facing areas.

**Why.** Children, especially under 8, struggle to recognise persuasive intent even when content is labelled. Recital 31 of the KIDS Act lists these tactics among those with particular persuasive effects on minors; UN General Comment 25 asks states to protect children from commercial exploitation.

**How to improve.** Remove brands and sponsored items from learning content; move partner credits to the teacher or guardian area.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [R-RADESKY2022](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/design-tricks-commonly-used-monetize-young-childrens-app-use)

### CORE-COM-09: Clear purchase information and a working right of withdrawal

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: purchases · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Before any purchase, with money or with purchasable currency, the buyer sees in plain words what is being bought, who sells it and how to contact them, the real-world price, whether and how the right of withdrawal applies, the legal guarantee, and how payment and delivery work. The buyer can withdraw within 14 days, and unused purchased currency can be returned in that time. For digital content the right is lost only after a separate, express consent to immediate delivery and an acknowledgement of losing it, confirmed afterwards. Paying with personal data does not remove it.

**Why.** Consumer Rights Directive Art. 6 (pre-contractual information) and Art. 9 to 16 (withdrawal), as the EU consumer authorities read them for games in CPC Key Principles 4 and 5. Missing purchase information and withdrawal rights are among the issues in the CPC Network's coordinated actions on games.

**How to improve.** Add an information screen before every purchase; add a 14-day withdrawal path, unused currency included; make the digital-content waiver a separate, explicit step and confirm it on the receipt.

**Sources.** [CRD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj), [CPC-VC](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [CPC-JS](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [UCPD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj)

### CORE-COM-10: Fair, plain terms for purchases and accounts

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: purchases · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Terms for the game, purchases and currency are in plain language and do not limit statutory rights. They do not let the trader remove or change bought content or currency, or change the currency's value, on its own; content that players can reasonably expect to keep stays available. An account ban, suspension or removal comes with a reason and a way to contest it.

**Why.** Unfair Contract Terms Directive Art. 3 and 5, as read by CPC Key Principle 6. For online platforms, DSA Art. 17 and 20 also require reasons and an internal complaint system for suspensions. Terms are written for adults; the child-friendly summary is in CORE-DAT-12.

**How to improve.** Rewrite currency and account terms in plain language; remove clauses that allow one-sided changes or removal; add a reasoned notice and an appeal for bans and suspensions.

**Sources.** [UCTD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1993/13/oj), [CPC-VC](https://commission.europa.eu/live-work-travel-eu/consumer-rights-and-complaints/enforcement-consumer-protection/coordinated-actions/social-media-online-games-and-search-engines_en), [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj)

### CORE-DAT-01: DPIA before launch

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** A Data Protection Impact Assessment exists before launch when children's data is processed at scale, with new technology (including AI), or for systematic monitoring of learners.

**Why.** Processing of vulnerable data subjects with new technology is high risk under GDPR Art. 35.

**How to improve.** Start a DPIA with templates/dpia-starter.md. If the school or Ministry is controller, provide them the technical input; they sign it.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-02: Controller and processor roles are defined, with processor agreements

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: low

**Requirement.** The manifest states whether the provider acts as controller or processor, and every third party that touches personal data has a data processing agreement (GDPR Art. 28).

**Why.** Without defined roles nobody is accountable for legal basis, DPIA or data subject requests.

**How to improve.** Record `gdpr_role` and `dpa_signed: true` for each third party, or remove the integration.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-03: No transfers outside the EEA without a valid mechanism

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Personal data of minors is hosted in the EEA, or every transfer outside it has a documented transfer mechanism (adequacy decision, SCCs plus transfer impact assessment).

**Why.** GDPR Chapter V.

**How to improve.** Move hosting to an EEA region or record `transfer_mechanism` for the third party.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-04: No personal data in analytics events

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Analytics and telemetry events carry no direct identifiers (name, email, phone, IP address, precise location, free text typed by the child). Use pseudonymous IDs.

**Why.** Data minimisation and purpose limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)(c)).

**How to improve.** Replace identifiers with a pseudonymous learner ID and drop free-text fields from events.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-05: Retention periods enforced by code

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Each category of learner data has a retention period, enforced by an automated deletion or anonymisation job, not only by policy text.

**Why.** Storage limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e)).

**How to improve.** Add a scheduled deletion job per data category and list it in csef.yaml `retention`.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-06: Data subject rights are supported by tooling

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Access, rectification, erasure and export of a learner's data can be executed by tooling (admin function or script), and the process is tested.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 15 to 20. Schools as controllers depend on the processor to execute requests.

**How to improve.** Build an admin export and delete function per learner and test it each release.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-07: No real learner data outside production

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Seeds, fixtures, tests, staging databases and prompts sent to development AI tools use synthetic data only.

**Why.** Purpose limitation and security (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)(f), Art. 32).

**How to improve.** Use a synthetic data generator (e.g. Faker) and block production dumps in non-production environments.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-08: No biometric identification of minors

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The product does not process face, voice or fingerprint data to identify children.

**Why.** Biometric data for identification is special category data (GDPR Art. 9). Disproportionate in education.

**How to improve.** Remove face or voice recognition. Use class codes, picture passwords or teacher-managed login.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-09: Geolocation off and not collected unless essential

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Precise geolocation is not collected. If a feature truly needs it, it is off by default and turned off again at the end of the session.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 11(1)(a) and 11(2) (applied to games via Art. 15(1)(b)). DSA Art. 28 guidelines on safe defaults.

**How to improve.** Remove location permissions or gate them behind an explicit, session-limited opt-in.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-10: Microphone and camera off by default

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Access to microphone and camera is off by default, requested only at the moment of use for a clear learning purpose, and the recording is not kept longer than needed.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 11(1)(b), applied to games via Art. 15(1)(b).

**How to improve.** Request media permissions just-in-time with a child-friendly explanation; never at start-up.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-11: Consent for non-essential storage and cookies

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Non-essential cookies and local storage are only set after valid consent. Where consent is the legal basis for a child below the national age of digital consent, the guardian gives it (see AGE-B4-01).

**Why.** ePrivacy Art. 5(3). The national consent age (GDPR Art. 8) is set out in AGE-B4-01.

**How to improve.** Keep only strictly necessary storage, or add a guardian-facing consent flow.

**Sources.** [EPRIV](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/58/oj), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [EDPB-CONSENT](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-052020-consent-under-regulation-2016679_en)

### CORE-DAT-12: Child-friendly privacy information

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Privacy information exists in a version the target age can understand (very short sentences, icons, audio for non-readers), plus a full version for adults.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 12(1) requires clear language, in particular for information addressed to a child.

**How to improve.** Write a one-screen child version of the privacy notice and test it with children of the target age.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-DAT-13: Every personal question has a recorded purpose and can be skipped

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: survey · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Each question asked to a child or guardian about the child's life, family, opinions, interests or feelings is listed in a survey register with its learning purpose, the closed answers, who answers it, who can see the answers, how long they are kept and the legal basis. Every question offers "prefer not to say" with the same weight as the other answers, the whole set can be skipped, no part of the product depends on answering, and answering earns no points, coins, badges or other rewards.

**Why.** Purpose limitation and data minimisation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)(c)) and data protection by design (Art. 25). A question without a purpose is data collected "just in case". Forcing, nudging or rewarding answers are deceptive design patterns (EDPB Guidelines 03/2022: skipping, stirring, obstructing), and a reward for telling turns disclosure into a game.

**How to improve.** Write the register from templates/survey-register.md, delete every question without a purpose, add "prefer not to say" and remove rewards for answering.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [EDPB-DDP](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-032022-deceptive-design-patterns-social-media_en), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-DAT-14: No personal data about other people is collected from children

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: survey, ugc, chat, ai_generative · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** The product does not ask children for the names, photos, voices, ages, jobs, health, whereabouts or contact details of relatives, friends or other people, and AI characters do not ask for them either. Where an activity needs such people, the child uses fictional characters or a generic role ("a grandparent"), and creation tools offer avatars instead of photos of real people.

**Why.** The other person is not informed and cannot exercise their rights (GDPR Art. 14), there is rarely a legal basis (Art. 6), and children cannot judge what is safe to tell about others. Details about relatives can also reveal special category data (see CORE-DAT-15).

**How to improve.** Replace name and detail fields about other people with fictional characters picked from a list, and tell AI prompts not to ask about real people.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-DAT-15: No questions that reveal special category data or family vulnerability

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: survey, ai_generative · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Children and guardians are not asked, directly or indirectly, about racial or ethnic origin, religion or beliefs, health or disability (of the child or of relatives), sexual orientation or political opinions, nor about family vulnerability: migration or residence status, parents' separation, bereavement, foster or residential care, income, debts or parents' jobs. Support needs are asked as product settings (bigger text, read-aloud, support language) chosen by the guardian or the child, never as a diagnosis or an origin. Mood check-ins are allowed only when the child picks the answer, it is not kept as a history per child (unless the child keeps it for themselves), it never becomes a label, and it is never inferred by AI (CORE-AI-01).

**Why.** Data that reveal a special category indirectly, by deduction or cross-referencing, fall under GDPR Art. 9 (CJEU C-184/20): an innocent family question can reveal religion, origin or health. Vulnerability data is not Art. 9 but is high risk: it can hurt the child, expose them to peers and adults, and calls for a DPIA (Art. 35). UN General Comment 25 protects children's privacy, including towards the adults around them.

**How to improve.** Remove these questions, turn diagnoses into settings, and keep low-risk closed questions or move the activity to fiction. If a question is truly needed, the controller (usually the school) decides it with a DPIA and an Art. 9(2) exception.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [CJEU-ART9](https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-184/20), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-DAT-16: Who answers personal questions fits the child's age

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: survey · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** For ages 3 to 9 (B1, B2), questions about the child's life are answered by a guardian with the child, not by the child alone. From 10, the child answers for themselves and guardians are told what is asked. From 13 (B4, B5), the child's answers about their opinions and feelings are not shown to guardians or teachers by default, unless the child chooses to share them or there is a safeguarding concern (CORE-CHT-08).

**Why.** Children's evolving capacities and their right to privacy, including towards parents (UN General Comment 25). Guardian tools in the EU KIDS Act proposal (Art. 20) must respect the child's privacy. Young children cannot yet weigh what they share; teenagers need a private space.

**How to improve.** Move questions for under-10s to the guardian page; for teenagers, keep answers private by default and say so.

**Sources.** [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-17: Teachers see answers about children's lives only as class totals

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: survey · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Teachers and schools see answers to personal questions only as totals for a group of at least 5 children per figure. A figure is hidden when it would still reveal a child: when every child gave the same answer, when two views differ by one child, or when filters narrow the group. Answers are never shown per child, on shared or projected screens, or in rankings. A per-child view exists only where the register's purpose requires it (for example, a child asks for help) and the child knows.

**Why.** Aggregation over small or uniform groups still identifies people (Article 29 Working Party Opinion 05/2014). Minimisation and data protection by default (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), 25(2)). Knowing a child's private life changes how adults and peers treat them. Extends B-OPS-01 to personal questions.

**How to improve.** Show only totals with a minimum group size, hide uniform or small cells, and remove per-child exports.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [WP216](https://ec.europa.eu/justice/article-29/documentation/opinion-recommendation/files/2014/wp216_en.pdf), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-DAT-18: Answers stay with their purpose and under the family's control

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: survey · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Answers are used only for the purpose in the register. They stay within the school's deployment and follow its instructions, are deleted at the end of the retention period, and are not used for advertising, profiling beyond the declared personalisation, AI training, or research unless B-DAT-01 is met and the approval is recorded. Personalisation based on the answers is explained to the child, shown to the guardian for children under 13, and can be changed or switched off. The child or guardian can see, correct and delete the answers at any time.

**Why.** Purpose limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)), rights of access, rectification and erasure (Art. 15 to 17), processor duties (Art. 28). Recital 71: decisions based on profiling should not concern a child. The EU KIDS Act proposal asks for high privacy by default for minors.

**How to improve.** Keep answers in the class instance, add see, correct and delete for answers, and make personalisation visible and reversible.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-DAT-19: Every logged event is declared in an event catalogue

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The product keeps an event catalogue (templates/event-catalogue.yaml) listing every gameplay or usage event it logs, each field of each event with its type, and the purpose it serves (operation, improvement, evaluation or research). Events and fields that are not in the catalogue are not sent. csef.yaml says whether the product logs events (`data_collection`) and links the catalogue.

**Why.** Purpose limitation and data minimisation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)(c)) and records of processing (Art. 30) need to know what is collected and why. Open Game Data's design goal "capture then analyze" is useful for research but collects more than a stated purpose needs; a catalogue turns it into "declare, then capture". The catalogue is also the allow-list that tooling/evidence.py checks event files against.

**How to improve.** Copy templates/event-catalogue.yaml, list every event with its fields and purpose, link it from csef.yaml, and remove logging calls that are not in it.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [R-OGD2024](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10593375)

### CORE-DAT-20: Player codes are random, scoped to one product and not derived from identifiers

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Event data uses a random player code made by the game or the server. It is never a hash or encoding of an email, name, username, account id or student number. A code is used in one product only and renewed each school year. Codes are not linked across products or providers, except inside a study with a recorded approval. The key between codes and accounts stays with the controller.

**Why.** A hash of a known value can be reversed by hashing likely values, so it is not effective pseudonymisation (GDPR Art. 4(5), EDPB Guidelines 01/2025). Codes shared across products enable profiling of children (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b), Recital 38). Keeping the key with the controller lets recipients receive data they cannot re-identify (CJEU, EDPS v SRB).

**How to improve.** Generate player codes with a secure random generator, store the link to accounts in a separate table, rotate codes each school year, and set cross_product_linking to false.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [EDPB-PSEUDO](https://edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2025/edpb-adopts-pseudonymisation-guidelines-and-paves-way-improve-cooperation_en), [CJEU-SRB](https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-413/23%20P)

### CORE-DAT-21: No fingerprinting attributes in telemetry

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Analytics and gameplay events do not carry device attributes that can single out a device: user agent strings, screen size or pixel ratio, installed fonts or plugins, hardware details, advertising ids (IDFA, GAID) or unique device ids. One coarse device class (tablet, laptop, desktop, phone, other) per session is enough for research and for teachers.

**Why.** Reading such attributes from the device to recognise it is access to terminal equipment under ePrivacy Art. 5(3) and needs consent unless strictly necessary (EDPB Guidelines 2/2023). Combined, they work as an identifier (GDPR Recital 30).

**How to improve.** Replace device attributes with one device class computed on the device, and remove advertising and unique device ids from events.

**Sources.** [EPRIV](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/58/oj), [EDPB-ART53](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-10/edpb_guidelines_202302_technical_scope_art_53_eprivacydirective_v2_en_0.pdf), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-DAT-22: Inferences about a child stay at population level by default

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Detectors that infer a state (stuck, frustrated, idle, likely to quit, ability) are used to improve the design for everyone, at population level. They are not shown as labels on a named child, used to rank children or used to decide for them, unless the product declares assessment and meets the assessment rules (A-ASM-01, B-EVL-01 to 04), and a teacher can see why and override. Emotion is never inferred from camera, voice or face.

**Why.** Inferences about a person are personal data. Labels on children invite surveillance and automated decisions (GDPR Art. 22, Recital 71); systems that evaluate learners are high-risk (AI Act Annex III) and emotion recognition in education is banned (AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)). The EU KIDS Act proposal and UN General Comment 25 ask for the child's best interests and privacy by default.

**How to improve.** Keep detector output in population features; if teachers need it, show class totals, or declare assessment and follow its rules.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [AIA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-DAT-23: No engagement targets for children

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Retention, daily or monthly active users, streak length, sessions per week or growth in playing time are not product targets, experiment goals or quality signals for children. Teams report learning, completion, help needed, accessibility and natural stopping points instead. Typical time to finish a unit may be measured to help teachers plan, never as a number to increase.

**Why.** The EU KIDS Act proposal bans design that leads to excessive use, and the Digital Fairness Act proposal targets features that keep minors engaged. Optimising for engagement pulls design towards those features. Engagement-based rewards lower intrinsic motivation and learning (Deci et al. 1999; Hanus and Fox 2015).

**How to improve.** Replace engagement KPIs in dashboards, experiments and OKRs with the csef-evidence-0.1 features.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act), [R-DECI1999](https://depts.washington.edu/techdocs/papers/deciExtrinsicRewardsAndIntrinsicMotivation99.pdf), [R-HANUS2015](https://www.smhp.psych.ucla.edu/pdfdocs/gamil.pdf)

### CORE-DAT-24: Open releases of learning data hold group figures only

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Data published openly (to a public site, repository or catalogue) holds population features only, in the csef-evidence-0.1 format: at least 10 players and 3 classes behind every figure, counts rounded to 5, dates to the month, no free text, no per-player, per-class or per-school rows, and no engagement metrics. Event-level and player-level data are never published, even with anonymous codes. When the data were collected as a processor for schools, the schools' contract allows the release.

**Why.** A stable player code with exact times can single out a child; small groups break aggregation (Article 29 Working Party, WP216). For the controller holding the key, pseudonymised data stay personal (CJEU, EDPS v SRB; EDPB Guidelines 01/2025), so publishing them is a disclosure of personal data. A processor may only process on the school's instructions (GDPR Art. 28(3)(a)).

**How to improve.** Publish with tooling/evidence.py build-feed and check every feed with check-feed before release.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [WP216](https://ec.europa.eu/justice/article-29/documentation/opinion-recommendation/files/2014/wp216_en.pdf), [CJEU-SRB](https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-413/23%20P), [EDPB-PSEUDO](https://edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2025/edpb-adopts-pseudonymisation-guidelines-and-paves-way-improve-cooperation_en)

### CORE-DAT-25: Research logging runs only in a study build

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Logging for research is off in the normal build. It runs in a study build with its own version branch (for example 2.1.0-study), given only to classes that agreed, under a data sharing agreement and an ethics approval, with a child-friendly notice and a way to leave the study without leaving the lesson. Device storage for research identifiers has a valid basis (consent where ePrivacy Art. 5(3) needs it).

**Why.** Research is a new purpose that needs a compatibility check and safeguards (GDPR Art. 6(4), 89). Storing or reading an identifier on the device for a purpose that is not strictly necessary needs consent under ePrivacy Art. 5(3) (EDPB Guidelines 2/2023). A separate build keeps the normal product within its purpose, and the version branch keeps study data apart (Open Game Data versioning).

**How to improve.** Add a study build flag that is off by default, record the agreement and approval in csef.yaml, and tag study builds with a version branch.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [EPRIV](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2002/58/oj), [EDPB-ART53](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-10/edpb_guidelines_202302_technical_scope_art_53_eprivacydirective_v2_en_0.pdf), [R-OGD2024](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10593375)

### CORE-DES-01: Motion and sound can be turned down or off

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** The product honours the device's reduced-motion setting and offers in-app controls to reduce animation and sound, including motion triggered by the learner's own actions.

**Why.** WCAG 2.3.3 (Level AAA) protects learners with vestibular disorders. Distracting motion and sound compete with the learning content for attention.

**How to improve.** Wrap animations in a reduced-motion check (CSS prefers-reduced-motion, useReducedMotion, platform accessibility APIs) and add 'calm mode' and sound sliders.

**Sources.** [W3C-233](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/animation-from-interactions.html), [WCAG22](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [R-SUNDARARAJAN2020](https://inspire.acu.edu.au/articles/seductive-details)

### CORE-DES-02: Motion shows the content, not decoration

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Animation is used to show what is learned (a process, a change over time, a procedure). Decorative, celebratory or purely entertaining motion and interesting-but-irrelevant extras ("seductive details") are kept to a minimum.

**Why.** Seductive details lower learning (g = -0.33, 58 studies). Animation that depicts the content improves it (g = 0.23, 140 comparisons). In e-books, story-carrying animation helps young children while hotspots and side games distract.

**How to improve.** For each animation, write down what it teaches. Remove or shorten the ones that teach nothing; move side games out of the learning path.

**Sources.** [R-SUNDARARAJAN2020](https://inspire.acu.edu.au/articles/seductive-details), [R-BERNEY2016](https://tecfa.unige.ch/perso/sandra/pdf/Earli2016_berney_betrancourt_FINAL.pdf), [R-TAKACS2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4647204)
