### CORE-DES-03: Calm screens, especially under 8

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: B1 (3-5), B2 (6-9) · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Few elements compete on screen at once (as a guide, no more than four interactive or animated elements on the main screen for under-8s), and help is available as audio or pictures, not text only.

**Why.** Busy visual environments increase off-task time in young children and affect autistic children most. A content analysis of 200 apps for under-8s found 95% showed more than four elements on the opening screen.

**How to improve.** Audit each screen's element count; move secondary elements into menus; add spoken help.

**Sources.** [R-FISHER2014](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01444/pdf), [R-HANLEY2017](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/output/1370163/classroom-displays-attraction-or-distraction-evidence-of-impact-on-attention-and-learning-from-children-with-and-without-autism), R-CAC2018, [R-HIRSHPASEK2015](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/educational-apps.html)

### CORE-DES-04: Fantasy does not blur facts for young children

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: B1 (3-5), B2 (6-9) · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** When teaching facts about the real world to young children, use realistic images and plain language. Talking animals, impossible events and fantasy framing are kept for stories and play, not for factual content.

**Why.** Human-like animals with human-like language reduced fact learning in 3 to 5-year-olds. Fantastical events, more than pace, reduced executive function in 4-year-olds.

**How to improve.** Review factual units for young children; replace anthropomorphic narration with realistic visuals or clearly separate story from fact.

**Sources.** [R-GANEA2014](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00283/full), [R-LILLARD2011](https://www.frontiersin.org/article/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.583174)

### CORE-DES-05: Visual style matches the concept, especially in maths

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Abstract concepts use simple, schematic visuals. Graphs and diagrams carry no decorative pictures. Concrete images are used to start, then faded towards abstract representations. Pleasant colours and friendly faces are welcome where they do not compete with the content.

**Why.** Pictures inside graphs led 6 to 8-year-olds to count the pictures; generic symbols transfer better than concrete ones. Schematic visuals outperform cartoon and realistic ones in learning games. Emotional design (pleasant colours, faces) improves retention (d = 0.39).

**How to improve.** Remove decoration from graphs and diagrams; plan concrete-to-abstract fading in maths sequences; keep warm, pleasant colour palettes.

**Sources.** [R-KAMINSKI2013](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/05/130508092412.htm), R-WOUTERS2013, [R-BROM2018](https://artemis.ms.mff.cuni.cz/main/papers/emodesign_manuscript_1rev_180928_FINAL_norev.pdf)

### CORE-DES-06: Celebrations are short and proportional

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Reward animations and sounds are brief, proportional to the achievement and skippable. Win sounds are not used to make small or no progress feel like a big win.

**Why.** Each celebration is itself a seductive detail competing for attention. In slot machines, win sounds made players overestimate how often they won.

**How to improve.** Cap celebration length (e.g. under 2 seconds), scale them to the achievement, and allow skipping.

**Sources.** [R-SUNDARARAJAN2020](https://inspire.acu.edu.au/articles/seductive-details), [R-DIXON2013](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/07/130702100348.htm)

### CORE-DES-07: No colour-psychology claims

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Design decisions and product claims do not rely on popular colour-psychology effects (e.g. "red lowers performance") that are not supported by robust evidence.

**Why.** The red-colour effect on cognitive performance does not survive correction for publication bias.

**How to improve.** Justify colour choices by function (contrast, coding, highlighting) and accessibility, not by colour-psychology claims.

**Sources.** [R-GNAMBS2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-020-01772-1)

### CORE-DES-08: Families and lives are shown without one default model

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Content about families, homes and daily life does not assume one model (a mother and a father, living grandparents, siblings, a room of one's own, holidays, money for extras). Every activity works with any answer, including "I don't have one" and "I'd rather not say", and families of many shapes appear in examples and illustrations. Themes such as loss, illness, separation or moving home come with a content note for the teacher, a calm exit for the child and a debrief.

**Why.** Children in care, bereaved, in single-parent, same-sex-parent or reconstituted families, or living in poverty should not feel excluded or have to explain themselves (non-discrimination, UN General Comment 25). Same aim as B-SIM-01, for every profile and every content type. Inclusion is one of the EU quality criteria for digital education content.

**How to improve.** Review family-themed content with a teacher and a school psychologist, add "I don't have one" paths, and add content notes for sensitive themes.

**Sources.** [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [EU-DEC](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/1fa0183b-dbbe-11f0-8da2-01aa75ed71a1/language-en), [ET4G2](https://www.unicef.org/digitaleducation/edtech-for-good)

### CORE-GOV-01: Product declares its CSEF manifest

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: low

**Requirement.** The repository contains a CSEF manifest (csef.yaml) declaring profiles, age bands, context of use, GDPR role, features, AI use, third parties and chosen compliance level.

**Why.** Accountability (GDPR Art. 5(2)) requires being able to show what the product does with children's data. The manifest is also what lets the checks select the right rules.

**How to improve.** Copy templates/csef.yaml to the repository root and fill it in with the product owner.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-GOV-02: Legal scope of the EU KIDS Act is assessed and recorded

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: low

**Requirement.** The manifest records whether the product is in scope of the EU KIDS Act (online game, AI companion, general conversational chatbot, social or video-sharing service) or exempt as a service designed primarily for education and operated by or on behalf of an educational establishment (Art. 2(4)(c)).

**Why.** The same product can be exempt when deployed by a school and in scope when offered directly to families. Teams must know which situation they are in for each channel.

**How to improve.** Fill the `legal_scope.kids_act` field in csef.yaml for each distribution channel.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [KIDS-FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/kids-act)

### CORE-GOV-03: Child rights impact assessment

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** A child rights impact assessment (or a risk review in the sense of the DSA Art. 28 guidelines) is documented, considers the best interests of the child, and involves children, guardians and educators in testing.

**Why.** The DSA guidelines and UN General Comment No. 25 ask providers to weigh all children's rights (protection, participation, provision), not only data protection.

**How to improve.** Extend the DPIA with a child rights section (templates/dpia-starter.md, part C).

**Sources.** [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation), [EUKO](https://www.lse.ac.uk/media-and-communications/research/research-projects/eu-kids-online)

### CORE-INT-01: Country rules are configuration, not code

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Rules that differ between countries live in per-country configuration, not in code: the age of digital consent and guardian consent steps, retention periods, national approvals (for example MIME in Portugal), safeguarding contacts and helplines, languages, school calendars and curriculum mappings. Each value has an owner and a source. An unknown country falls back to the most protective value. Adding a country is a configuration change and a review, not a code change.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 8 lets each Member State set the age of digital consent between 13 and 16, and national rules on school surveys, safeguarding and retention differ. A product sold in several countries, or offered through shared infrastructure such as the EDU-EDIC, needs these differences to be explicit, reviewable and testable. Hard-coded values silently apply one country's rules everywhere.

**How to improve.** Move country-specific values into one versioned file per country, reference it as `country_config` in csef.yaml, and default to the strictest value.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [EDU-EDIC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202602413)

### CORE-INT-02: Schools can take their data and leave

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The school, or whoever buys the product, can export all of its data at class and school level in documented, machine-readable open formats: rosters, results, learner-created work and settings, with the schema published. Where the product exchanges data with school systems it uses open standards (OneRoster for rosters and results, LTI 1.3 for launching from a learning platform). The exit process is documented with timelines, and switching costs nothing beyond the subscription.

**Why.** Data Act Chapter VI gives customers of data processing services, SaaS included, a right to switch and prohibits switching charges from 12 January 2027 (Art. 29). GDPR Art. 20 covers portability for each learner (CORE-DAT-06). Interoperable infrastructure and less lock-in are aims of the EDU-EDIC.

**How to improve.** Add a school-level export in CSV or JSON with a published schema (OneRoster where it fits), describe the exit process in the contract, and test a full export each release.

**Sources.** [DATA-ACT](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2854/oj), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [1EDTECH](https://www.1edtech.org/standards/oneroster), [EDU-EDIC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202602413)

### CORE-INT-03: Sign-in and rosters come from the school, with the minimum data

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Features: accounts · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** In schools, learners and teachers sign in through the school's identity provider (OpenID Connect or SAML) or are launched from the school's learning platform (LTI 1.3), instead of creating separate product accounts. Roster imports carry only the fields the product needs (no birth dates, addresses or national identity numbers unless a rule requires them), and learner records use pseudonymous identifiers.

**Why.** Fewer separate accounts mean fewer stored passwords and less personal data (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) and 25). Standard sign-in and launch let the same product run in several countries and on shared infrastructure such as the EDU-EDIC without rebuilding each integration.

**How to improve.** Support OpenID Connect sign-in and LTI 1.3 launch, trim roster imports to the minimum fields, and key learner records on pseudonymous IDs.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [1EDTECH](https://www.1edtech.org/standards/oneroster), [EDU-EDIC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202602413)

### CORE-INT-04: Critical dependencies are declared and replaceable

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Every third party records where it is established (`jurisdiction`) as well as where it hosts data (`region`), and whether the product stops working without it (`critical`). A critical provider established outside the EU or EEA, AI model providers included, has a documented `fallback`: an alternative established in the EU behind the same internal interface, or a reduced mode that keeps learning available. Features call AI models through one internal interface, so a school or a country can require a different model.

**Why.** Data hosted in the EU may still be reachable under the laws of the provider's home country, and one provider changing its terms or leaving can stop a product used by thousands of schools. Reducing structural dependencies on third-country providers is an aim of the EDU-EDIC. Builds on CORE-DAT-02 (processor agreements) and CORE-DAT-03 (transfers).

**How to improve.** Add `jurisdiction`, `critical` and `fallback` to each third party in csef.yaml, put AI calls behind one internal interface, and test the fallback once a year.

**Sources.** [EDU-EDIC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202602413), [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-SAF-01: Most protective settings by default

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Profiles private, sharing off, contact off, notifications off, recommendations of other users off by default. The product never relaxes these defaults on its own. Only an adult, or a 16 or 17 year old after clear information and an explicit choice (AGE-B5-01), can change them.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 8(1) and 11(1). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.

**How to improve.** Flip the defaults in the settings model and add a test that asserts them.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)

### CORE-SAF-02: Notifications only about the child's own activity, off by default, quiet hours

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: notifications · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Push notifications are off by default, never designed to prompt the child to start or resume use, only relate to the child's own activity or teacher assignments, and respect school time and core sleep hours.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 9(2)(b) and 11(1)(d), applied to games via Art. 15(1).

**How to improve.** Default the push flag to false, remove re-engagement campaigns, add quiet hours (e.g. 21:00 to 08:00 and school hours).

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act)

### CORE-SAF-03: Natural stopping points, no autoplay or endless feeds

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** No autoplay of the next content and no infinite scroll. Sessions have natural endings and regular interruption moments that let the child decide whether to continue.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 9(2)(a). DFA proposal gives users the right to switch off autoplay.

**How to improve.** Remove autoplay; end each activity with a clear 'done' screen and an explicit choice to continue.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DFA](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [R-RADESKY2022](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/design-tricks-commonly-used-monetize-young-childrens-app-use)

### CORE-SAF-04: Time-awareness tools

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** The product offers break reminders and lets guardians or teachers set a daily time limit, protecting school time (outside class use) and core sleep hours.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 9(3) and 20(4)(a) require time-limited access for social and video services. Best practice for all products.

**How to improve.** Add a session timer with a gentle break screen and a configurable daily limit.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [KIDS-COM](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0680)

### CORE-SAF-05: No contact from strangers; play stays in closed groups

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc · Detection: mixed · Effort: high

**Requirement.** Nobody outside the child's approved group (class, guardian-approved contacts) can initiate contact, see the child's profile or content, or add the child to a group. Multiplayer happens in groups set up by a teacher or guardian; play across groups only through pairing arranged by adults. The product cannot be used to lure children to other services.

**Why.** DSA Art. 28 and guidelines. KIDS Act Art. 12(1), applied to games via Art. 15(1)(c) and 15(2). Merges A-SOC-01 (retired in 0.11.0).

**How to improve.** Scope all interaction to closed groups managed by a teacher or guardian (class rooms with join codes); remove user search and contact suggestions; block external links and handles (CORE-CHT-05).

**Sources.** [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-SAF-06: Reports are acknowledged, answered and followed by help

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Features: chat, multiplayer, social, ugc, ai_generative · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Wherever children interact with others or with generated content, they can report it, AI output included. After a report the child (1) sees at once, in words for their age, that it arrived, what happens next and when; (2) gets help information straight away (a trusted adult, the national helpline); (3) is told the outcome when it is handled, without details about other children ("we took action", or "we looked and did not find a problem, and this is why"); and (4) can say "it is still happening", which reopens the report. Reports from minors are handled first.

**Why.** DSA Art. 16(5) requires telling the person who reported about the decision without undue delay. KIDS Act Art. 19 asks for child-friendly reporting and support. Children stop reporting when nothing seems to happen. The report and block tools themselves are in CORE-CHT-02.

**How to improve.** Add an acknowledgement screen and an outcome message in child language, a "still happening" button that reopens the case, and a measure of time from report to outcome.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [CB-AP](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/news/eu-action-plan-against-cyberbullying)

### CORE-SAF-07: Tools for guardians and teachers that respect the child

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: high

**Requirement.** Guardians (or teachers in school use) can manage settings, time and contacts. The child is told when such tools are active. Controls cannot be bypassed by the child.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 20, applied to online games by Art. 15(1)(d).

**How to improve.** Provide a guardian or teacher panel for settings, time limits and contacts, with an in-app notice to the child.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-SAF-08: Proportionate, privacy-preserving age assurance

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: high

**Requirement.** Where age matters, age assurance is proportionate, uses zero-knowledge solutions such as the EU age verification app, does not store identity documents and only keeps an age signal. Self-declaration alone is not relied on for high-risk features.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 27 and 28: age assurance must be accurate and privacy-preserving, and its data may never be used to identify, track, target, advertise to or profile the user (Art. 28(1)). Art. 31 requires Member States to provide free EU age verification and guardian attestation means. DSA Art. 28 guidelines. EU age verification Recommendation.

**How to improve.** Integrate the EU age verification solution or the EUDI wallet, and the national guardian attestation when available (KIDS Act Art. 31); store only an 'over threshold' flag and never reuse age assurance data for any other purpose.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors), [AVREC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-urges-member-states-rollout-eu-age-verification-app)

### CORE-SAF-09: Children can control and give feedback on what they see

**SHOULD** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: B3 (10-12), B4 (13-15), B5 (16-17) · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Children can adjust settings that affect how they interact and what they are shown, give feedback with lasting effect, and easily return to default settings.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 18.

**How to improve.** Add a simple 'my settings' screen with a 'reset to safe settings' button.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681), [UNCRC-GC25](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/general-comments-and-recommendations/general-comment-no-25-2021-childrens-rights-relation)

### CORE-SAF-10: No social comparison or image-altering features

**MUST** · Level 2 (Forward-compliant) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** No follower counts, likes on the child's appearance, beauty filters, or features that embellish or idealise the child's image.

**Why.** KIDS Act Art. 11(3).

**How to improve.** Remove public counters and appearance filters; use avatars instead of photos.

**Sources.** [KIDS](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0681)

### CORE-SEC-01: No secrets in the repository

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** API keys, tokens and passwords are not committed.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 32 (security of processing).

**How to improve.** Rotate the exposed key, move it to a secret manager, and add gitleaks to CI.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-SEC-02: Access control on every store of learner data

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: mixed · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Every table, bucket or collection with learner data enforces access control at the data layer (e.g. row-level security), not only in the client.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 25 and 32. Client-only checks are easily bypassed.

**How to improve.** Enable row-level security with policies scoped to class and role; add a test per table.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-SEC-03: Encryption in transit

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** All network calls use TLS. No plain http endpoints for APIs or assets.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 32.

**How to improve.** Switch the URL to https and enable HSTS.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-SEC-04: No personal data in logs

**SHOULD** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: static · Effort: low

**Requirement.** Application logs contain pseudonymous IDs only, with short retention.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) and 32. Logs are often copied to third-party tools.

**How to improve.** Log the learner ID instead of names or emails; add a log scrubber.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj)

### CORE-SEC-05: Vulnerability handling and breach response

**MUST** · Level 1 (Legal baseline) · Age bands: all · Detection: manifest · Effort: low

**Requirement.** A published way to report vulnerabilities (SECURITY.md or security.txt), a process to fix them, and a breach procedure that lets controllers meet the 72-hour notification deadline.

**Why.** GDPR Art. 33. Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations for products with digital elements.

**How to improve.** Add SECURITY.md and an incident runbook with contact chain and timelines.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [CRA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj)

### CORE-SEC-06: Strong authentication for adults, simple safe login for children

**SHOULD** · Level 3 (Best practice) · Age bands: all · Detection: manual · Effort: medium

**Requirement.** Teacher and admin accounts use MFA. Children use age-appropriate login (class code, picture password, teacher reset) without email or phone collection.

**Why.** Adult accounts hold data on whole classes. Children should not need personal contact details to log in.

**How to improve.** Enforce MFA for staff roles; replace child email login with class codes.

**Sources.** [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), [DSA-G28](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)
